subject: Cooking
title: The Economics of Street Food
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Economics of Street Food.

hook.text: A Bangkok pad thai vendor earns more per square foot than many sit-down restaurants. No rent. No waitstaff.

buildup.text: Street food economics are brutal but efficient — low overhead, high volume, razor-thin margins per item.

discovery.text: A typical vendor serves 200–500 customers daily, spending 60–70% of revenue on ingredients alone.

twist.text: Many vendors earn more than minimum wage workers but have zero benefits, insurance, or retirement savings.

climax.text: In Lagos, Mexico City, and Mumbai, street food employs millions who'd otherwise have no income at all.

punchline.text: Street food is cheap for you and hard for them. The margins are razor-thin.

quiz.question: What percentage of revenue do typical street food vendors spend on ingredients?

details.summary: Street food employs an estimated 10 million vendors worldwide, mostly women and immigrants. Startup costs as low as $100 make it the most accessible food business. Margins are razor-thin — vendors rely on volume and minimal waste.
details.whyItMatters: Street food is one of the world's largest informal employment sectors. Understanding its economics shows how food entrepreneurship provides pathways out of poverty with minimal barriers to entry.
takeaways: An estimated 10 million street food vendors operate worldwide
Startup costs can be as low as $100 for a basic street setup
Women and immigrants dominate the street food vendor workforce

faq.question: Why is street food dominated by women and immigrants?
faq.answer: Low startup costs eliminate the financial barriers that keep marginalized groups out of formal business. Cooking skills transfer directly from home to commerce. Flexible hours accommodate family care responsibilities. Immigrants bring culinary knowledge that creates market differentiation.

faq.question: How much do street food vendors typically earn?
faq.answer: Earnings vary enormously by location. In developing countries, vendors may earn $5 to $20 per day. In Western cities, established food trucks can gross $500 to $2,000 daily. Margins run 10 to 30 percent. Success depends on location, specialization, and consistent quality driving repeat customers.
